However, this book was without much doubt a posthumous collection, including various poems, prose, and administrative documents written by Shen.<ref name="sivin 1995 III 48"/> By the 15th century (during the [[Ming dynasty]]), this book was reprinted, yet only the 19th chapter remained.<ref name="sivin 1995 III 48"/> This chapter was reprinted in 1718, yet poorly edited.<ref name="sivin 1995 III 48"/> Finally, in the 1950s the author Hu Daojing supplemented this small yet valuable work with additions of other scattered poems written by Shen, in the former's ''Collection of Shen Kua's Extant Poetry'' (Shanghai: Shang-hai Shu-tian, 1958).<ref name="sivin 1995 III 48"/> In the tradition of the popular Song era literary category of 'travel record literature' ('youji wenxue'),<ref name="hargett 1985 67">{{harvnb|Hargett |1985|p=67}}</ref> Shen Kuo also wrote the ''Register of What Not to Forget'', a [[travel literature|traveler's guide]] to what type of [[carriage]] is suitable for a journey, the proper foods one should bring, the special clothing one should bring, and many other items.<ref name="hargett 1985 71">{{harvnb|Hargett |1985|p=71}}</ref>

In his ''Sequel to Numerous Things Revealed'', the Song author Cheng Dachang (1123–1195) noted that stanzas prepared by Shen Kuo for military victory celebrations were later written down and published by Shen.<ref name="stock 1993 94">{{harvnb|Stock|1993|p=94}}</ref> This includes a short poem "Song of Triumph" by Shen Kuo, who uses the musical instrument ''[[huqin|mawei huqin]]'' ('horse-tail barbarian stringed instrument' or 'horse-tail fiddle'<ref>{{harvnb|Stock|1993|p= 108}}</ref>) of the northwestern [[Inner Asia]]n nomads as a metaphor for prisoners-of-war led by Song troops:
{{Centered pull quote
| The ''mawei huqin'' followed the Han chariot,
Its music sounding of complaint to the Khan.

Do not bend the bow to shoot the goose within the clouds,
The returning goose bears no letter.
| author = Shen Kuo<ref name="stock 1993 94"/>
}}
Historian Jonathan Stock notes that the bent bow described in the poem above represents the arched bow used to play the ''huqin'', while the sound of the instrument itself represented the discontent expressed by the prisoners-of-war with their defeated [[Khan (title)|khan]].<ref name="stock 1993 94"/>

== Legacy ==
[[File:Shen Kua sketch.jpg|thumb|A sketch of Shen Kuo by an anonymous artist of the [[Qing dynasty]], 18th century]]

=== Praise, critique, and criticism ===
In the ''Routledge Curzon Encyclopedia of Confucianism'', Xinzhong Yao states that Shen Kuo's legacy was tainted by his eager involvement in Wang Anshi's New Policies reforms, his actions criticized in [[Twenty-Four Histories|the later traditional histories]].<ref name="yao 2003 544"/> However, Shen's reputation as a polymath has been well regarded. Joseph Needham stated that Shen Kuo was "one of the greatest scientific minds in Chinese history."<ref>{{harvnb|Fraser| Haber|1986|pp=226–227}}</ref> The [[French people|French]] sinologist [[Jacques Gernet]] is of the opinion that Shen possessed an "amazingly modern mind."<ref name="gernet 1996 338">{{harvnb|Gernet|1996|p=338}}</ref> Yao states of Shen's thorough recording of natural sciences in his ''Dream Pool Essays'':

<blockquote>
We must regard Shen Kuo's collection as an indispensable primary source attesting to the unmatched level of attainment achieved by Chinese science prior to the twelfth century.<ref name="yao 2003 545">{{harvnb|Yao|2003|p=545}}</ref>
</blockquote>

However, Toby E. Huff writes that Shen Kuo's "scattered set" of writings lacks clear-cut organization and "theoretical acuteness," that is, [[scientific theory]].<ref name="huff 2003 303">{{harvnb|Huff|2003|p=303}}</ref> Nathan Sivin wrote that Shen's originality stands "cheek by jowl with trivial didacticism, court anecdotes, and ephemeral curiosities" that provide little insight.<ref name="huff 2003 303"/> Donald Holzman writes that Shen "has nowhere organized his observations into anything like a general theory."<ref name="huff 2003 303"/> Huff writes that this was a systemic problem of early Chinese science, which lacked systematic treatment that could be found in European works such as the ''Concordance and Discordant Canons'' by the lawyer [[Gratian (jurist)|Gratian]] of [[Bologna]] (fl. 12th century).<ref name="huff 2003 303"/> In regard to an overarching concept of [[science]] which could branch together all the various sciences studied by the Chinese, Sivin asserts that the writings of Shen Kuo "do not indicate that he achieved, or even sought, an integrated framework for his diverse knowledge; the one common thread is the varied responsibilities of his career as a high civil servant."<ref>{{harvnb|Sivin|1988|p=59}}</ref>

=== Burial and posthumous honors ===
Upon his death, Shen Kuo was interred in a tomb in [[Yuhang]] District of [[Hangzhou]], at the foot of the Taiping Hill.<ref name="Yuhang">
Yuhang Cultural Network (October 2003). [http://www.yhwt.com/newsshow.aspx?artid=3169 Shen Kuo's Tomb] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140502074744/http://www.yhwt.com/newsshow.aspx?artid=3169 |date=2014-05-02 }}  The Yuhang District of Hangzhou Cultural Broadcasting Press and Publications Bureau. Retrieved on 2007-05-06.
</ref> His tomb was eventually destroyed, yet [[Ming dynasty]] records indicated its location, which was found in 1983 and protected by the government in 1986.<ref name="Yuhang" /> The remnants of the tomb's brick structure remained, along with Song dynasty [[glass]]wares and [[coin]]s.<ref name="Yuhang" /> The Hangzhou Municipal Committee completed a restoration of Shen's tomb in September 2001.

In addition to his tomb, Shen Kuo's ''Mengxi'' garden estate, his former two-acre (8,000 m<sup>2</sup>) property in Zhenjiang, was restored by the government in 1985.<ref name="Talking Park">
Zhenjiang.gov (October 2006). [http://www.zhenjiang.gov.cn/gb/zgzj/zjgb/lyzpd/fjjc/userobject1ai12068.html Talking Park] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070707034017/http://www.zhenjiang.gov.cn/gb/zgzj/zjgb/lyzpd/fjjc/userobject1ai12068.html |date=2007-07-07 }}  The Zhenjiang municipal government office. Retrieved on 2007-05-07.
</ref> However, the renovated Mengxi Garden is only part of the original of Shen Kuo's time.<ref name="Mengxi Garden">
The Zhenjiang Foreign Experts Bureau (June 2002). [http://www.feb.gov.cn/news1/displaynews.asp?id=139 Mengxi Garden] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929042332/http://www.feb.gov.cn/news1/displaynews.asp?id=139 |date=2007-09-29 }}  The Zhenjiang Foreign Experts Bureau. Retrieved on 2007-05-07.
</ref> A [[Qing dynasty]]-era hall built on the site is now used as the main admissions gate.<ref name="Talking Park" /> In the Memorial Hall of the gardens, there is a large painting depicting the original garden of Shen Kuo's time, including wells, green bamboo groves, stone-paved paths, and decorated walls of the original halls.<ref name="Mengxi Garden" /> In this exhibition hall there stands a 1.4&nbsp;m (4.6&nbsp;ft) tall statue of Shen Kuo sitting on a platform, along with centuries-old published copies of his ''Dream Pool Essays'' in glass cabinets, one of which is from Japan.<ref name="Mengxi Garden" /> At the garden estate there are also displayed marble banners, statues of Shen Kuo, and a model of an armillary sphere; a small museum gallery depicts Shen's various achievements.<ref name="Talking Park" />

The [[Purple Mountain Observatory]] in [[Nanjing]] discovered a new [[asteroid]] in 1964 and named it after Shen Kuo ([[2027 Shen Guo]]).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://minorplanetcenter.net/db_search/show_object?object_id=2027|title=2027 Shen Guo|last=|first=|date=|publisher=IAU Minor Planet Center|access-date=2018-10-01}}</ref>
